title: Lesson 90 - The Two Experts Don't Quite Agree

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: My first note says, “Imani recommends a phased migration, but Julian wants a single cutover.” It sounds as if they disagree about everything.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: They do not. Both experts agree that the original archive must remain unchanged, every imported batch must be checked and a rollback copy must exist before public access changes.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: They also agree that the three-hundred-record test should happen before any full decision.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Yes. According to Imani, the test should be followed by several small batches so mapping errors can be isolated and corrected before the next batch.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: Julian argues that a long parallel period creates duplicate staff work and two changing versions of the catalog.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Where they differ is the stage after the test, not whether accuracy or rollback matters.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: Imani places more weight on limiting the size of any one error. Julian places more weight on limiting the time staff must operate two systems.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: That is a better comparison than “cautious expert versus fast expert.” Both are managing risk; they prioritize different kinds.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: Does Julian dismiss the risk of mapping errors?

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: No. His note proposes a forty-eight-hour public freeze, a complete validation run and a prepared rollback. He thinks concentrated checking is more controllable than repeated small cutovers.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: That doesn’t necessarily contradict Imani’s preservation rule. He accepts the same unchanged source copy and validation requirement.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Correct. Imani questions whether one validation weekend gives staff enough time to spot subtle description errors across different collections.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: The disagreement turns on whether smaller error exposure is worth several weeks of parallel work.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: And our current briefing does not estimate the staffing cost of parallel work or the rate of subtle errors in the test batch.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: So I cannot conclude that either approach is cheaper or safer overall.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Right. You can report which risk each approach reduces and which new burden it creates.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: Here’s the short version for the meeting: both experts require an unchanged source, validation and rollback. Imani supports staged batches to contain errors; Julian supports one controlled cutover to reduce parallel work.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Add the evidence gap: the test must tell us about error type and review time before the trade-off can be assessed.

lines.speaker: Robin
lines.text: I’ve left out their software preferences because neither recommendation depends on a specific brand in this exercise.

lines.speaker: Keira
lines.text: Good. A neutral synthesis gives decision-makers the shared floor, the real hinge and the missing evidence—not a winner chosen by the summarizer.
